titleStmt.title: An Abstract Interpretation-Based Framework for WCET Analysis of Parallel Programs

analytic.title: An Abstract Interpretation-Based Framework for WCET Analysis of Parallel Programs

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Estimating the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of programs in an embedded multi-core environment is fundamental for schedulability analysis. In this paper, we propose a framework for calculating the WCET of programs originally designed for single-core systems when migrated to and executed in parallel on multi-core environments. First, we decompose single-core tasks and convert them into parallel programs using OpenMP. Our approach extends the task dependency graph to describe relevant information for parallel tasks (such as execution time estimation, core allocation, and inter-task dependencies). Finally, we present an iterative algorithm based on abstract interpretation. This algorithm takes the parallel task dependency graph as input and uses fixed-point analysis to determine the WCET of parallel programs. We conducted experiments on a physical machine to verify the feasibility of our solution.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the increasing performance demands of embedded real-time systems, multi-core processors are becoming more prevalent. Accurately estimating the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of programs in an embedded multi-core environment is crucial for schedulability analysis and ensuring the safety and reliability of these systems [1]. Traditional WCET analysis methods designed for single-core processors do not suffice for the complexities introduced by multicore architectures, where concurrent execution and inter-core communication add layers of unpredictability.

In recent years, significant research has been conducted to address the challenges of WCET estimation in multi-core systems [1]- [8]. Several approaches have been proposed to model the intricacies of multi-core execution environments. Wilhelm et al. provide an extensive overview of WCET analysis methods and tools, highlighting the complexities introduced by shared resources such as caches and buses in multi-core systems [9]. Davis and Burns survey hard real-time scheduling for multiprocessor systems, discussing the implications of multicore architectures on timing predictability [10]. Altmeyer and Davis further explore the contention sensitivity in multicore hardware platforms, presenting methods to mitigate the unpredictability caused by resource sharing [11]. Tools such as OTAWA [12] and Heptane [13] have been instrumental in advancing static WCET analysis techniques. These tools provide frameworks for timing analysis that can handle the increased complexity of modern embedded systems. Additionally, the adoption of parallel programming models like OpenMP has been suggested to enhance the scalability and efficiency of WCET analysis. Marongiu and Benini demonstrate the use of OpenMP to effectively manage distributed scratchpad memory in multi-processor systems on chip (MPSoCs), which is crucial for optimizing performance and predictability [14], [15]. Despite these advancements, accurately estimating WCET in a multi-core environment remains a significant challenge due to the need to account for parallel task execution and schedule category. This paper introduces several innovations to address these challenges:

• Decomposition and Parallelization Framework: We propose a novel framework for transitioning single-core programs to multi-core environments. This framework begins with the decomposition of single-core tasks and their transformation into parallel programs using OpenMP, a widely adopted API for parallel programming. The iterative nature of our algorithm allows it to refine WCET estimations progressively, converging to a precise value that reflects the worst-case scenario.

We validate our framework through extensive experiments on actual hardware, demonstrating its effectiveness and practicality. Our experiments involve well-known embedded applications, including the Gaussian blur algorithm, serving as benchmarks to compare our WCET estimations with actual execution times. The results confirm the feasibility of our approach, providing a reliable method for WCET estimation in multi-core embedded systems. By bridging the gap between single-core and multi-core WCET analysis, our framework offers a robust solution for the growing complexity of embedded real-time systems, ensuring their performance and reliability in multi-core environments.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARY
div.p: Abstract interpretation [16] is a theory used in static program analysis to provide sound approximations of a program's behavior. The primary goal of abstract interpretation is to derive properties of a program that hold for all possible executions. This is achieved by mapping concrete program states to an abstract domain, which simplifies the analysis while preserving essential properties relevant to the program's execution. Formally, abstract interpretation involves the following components:
• Concrete Domain (C): The set of all possible states that a program can reach during its execution.
• Abstract Domain (A): A simplified representation of the concrete domain that retains essential information for the analysis.
• Abstraction Function (α : C → A): A mapping from the concrete domain to the abstract domain.

• Concretization Function (γ : A → C): A mapping from the abstract domain back to the concrete domain. • Abstract Operations: Operations defined on the abstract domain that correspond to concrete operations in the program.

The abstraction and concretization functions form a Galois connection, ensuring that the analysis is sound, i.e., the properties derived in the abstract domain are valid in the concrete domain. Fixed-point analysis is a crucial step in implementing static analysis. Its goal is to find a state such that, when the program's transfer function is applied to this state, it remains unchanged. For abstract interpretation, fixed-point analysis is typically used to compute the fixed point of a program's control flow graph or data flow graph, thereby determining all possible program states or data flow information.

This paper proposes an iterative algorithm based on abstract interpretation for computing the WCET of parallel programs. Through fixed-point analysis, the algorithm estimates the latest start and finish times for each task, ultimately determining the WCET of the entire parallel program.

div.head: III. METHODS
div.p: In this section, we describe how to parallelize serial tasks and provide an algorithm for WCET analysis of parallel programs on multi-core systems, as illustrated in the flowchart in Figure 1. The algorithm process primarily includes preprocessing the source program (such as removing comments and unnecessary input/output), decomposing and parallelizing serial tasks, generating the parallel task dependency graph, and calculating the WCET of the multi-core program using an iterative algorithm based on abstract interpretation. The following subsections will provide a detailed description of each module:

div.head: Fig. 2. Chronos analysis process
div.p: A. Single-core WCET analysis

The development of single-core WCET analysis techniques has reached a mature stage [17], encompassing control flow analysis, microprocessor modeling, and WCET computation: In this paper, we use Chronos [18], an open-source tool developed by NUS, to estimate the WCET of single tasks. Chronos uses static analysis techniques to get an estimation of the WCET of a program, which is called WCET Est. Meanwhile, Chronos employs SimpleScalar [19] to simulate the program, considering the impact of caches, instruction sets, and other factors on WCET, and the result is called WCET Sim. The Users can configure SimpleScalar processor model information according to their needs, such as cache block size, and in-order or out-of-order pipelines. Additionally, users can manually add constraints like loop bounds. The detailed process is illustrated in Figure 2. Our method extends the formal definitions of parallel tasks and the corresponding task graph syntax and semantics based on the OmpTG tool [20], and provides the instance declarations of parallel tasks.

div.p: We consider a parallel task system consisting of n tasks {τ 1 , . . . , τ n }. This method mainly focuses on task-level dependency abstraction and does not consider the internal control flow of tasks. A real-time task system τ can be represented by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G = (V, E, l), where V represents the set of vertices, E represents the set of edges, and ↕ represents the mapping function of node attributes.

A vertex is represented as a task in V , and there are two types, the normal task type V N and the waiting task type V T W , where V T W denotes the node representation of the task waiting dependency, and V N denotes a normal task, V = V N ∪ V T W .

The edge E in G only represents the dependencies in tasks, and the dependencies are divided into three types: sequential relationships E N , which represent the order of execution of tasks; the dispatch relationship E D , which indicates that the task creates a new task and the synchronization relationship E S , which means waiting for the completion of the preceding task, is connected with the node V T W . The mapping function l of node attributes can be represented by l : v ∈ V N → A × C × T , where A represents the name of the task, C represents the processor resources assigned to the task, and T is a real number greater than 0 representing the execution time of the task.

div.head: C. Iterative algorithm based on abstract interpretation
div.p: After obtaining the WCET for each task and generating the parallel task dependency graph, the problem can be abstracted as finding the longest path weight in a graph with known start and end points. To address this, we propose an iterative algorithm based on abstract interpretation. First, we define the following:

For a given task t, we define L F [t] as the latest finish time of task t, and L R[t] as the latest time by which all predecessor tasks of t are completed. The WCET of the entire program is the time from the L R[t begin ] of the start node to the L F [t end ] of the end node. Therefore, the WCET calculation for the entire parallel program is given by Equation (1).
div.formula: W CET = L F [t end ] -L R[t begin ](1)
div.p: The calculation of the L R[t] for task t is given by Equation ( 2), where P represents the set of predecessor tasks of t.
If there are no tasks concurrently executing on the same core as task t, the calculation formula for L F [t] is given by Equation ( 3):
div.formula: L F [t] = L R[t] + W CET [t](3)
div.p: If there exists a task set S, where all tasks execute on one core and there are conflicting relationships ,the calculation of L F [t] for task t is shown in Equation ( 4).
div.formula: L F [t] = L R[t] + W CET [t] + t′∈S W CET [t′](4)
div.p: Through the analysis above, we can compute the L R[t] and L F [t] for each task t using the iterative algorithm based on abstract interpretation. The specific algorithm is shown in Algorithm 1.

Complexity analysis: The algorithm involves nested iterations over all nodes in the graph, updating L F [t] and L R[t] based on dependencies until a fixed point is reached. The complexity analysis indicates a time complexity of O(n 2 ) where is the number of nodes in the graph, with additional considerations for iterations and space complexity of O(n).

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTS A. Experimental Setup
div.p: Benchmark: The benchmark selected in this article is the Gaussian blur algorithm, which is widely used in the embedded domain for tasks such as image denoising, image smoothing, and feature extraction. The Gaussian blur program includes reading the Gaussian kernel and image information, performing calculations using the Gaussian blur algorithm, and generating the blurred image, as shown in Figure 4. This article focuses on parallelizing the Gaussian blur calculation process and performance evaluation, which will be discussed in more detail in the next subsection.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: In the Gaussian blur algorithm, the computations between individual pixels are independent of each other. Therefore, we use a striping partition algorithm to divide parallel tasks based on the image matrix's height and the number of processors. We assume that the Gaussian image pixel matrix consists of n rows and that there are currently p processor cores. The algorithm allocates n/p rows of the pixel matrix to each processor core, allowing the p processors to handle tasks in parallel. The parallel task dependency graph of the resulting program is shown in Figure 3, which was analysed in section III.

The detailed description of single task nodes is provided in Table II, where a 1 to a 4 represent the initialization program, From Table III, it is evident that through parallel optimization, the WCET of the parallel program is significantly smaller than that of the serial program. In multi-level loop programs, if the iteration count can be predetermined, the accuracy of the WCET estimation is relatively high.

The experimental results suggest that in a multi-core environment, without considering L2 cache or assuming each core has its independent L2 cache, and without considering interprocess communication and locking mechanisms, it is possible to estimate the WCET of parallel programs accurately.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This paper introduces a framework for migrating singlecore programs to multi-core embedded real-time systems. It utilizes OpenMP for parallelizing serial programs and OpmTG for generating parallel task dependency graphs. An iterative algorithm based on abstract interpretation is proposed to use these graphs for determining the best and worst-case execution times of tasks, thereby calculating the WCET of the entire parallel program. The Gaussian blur algorithm, used as a benchmark, demonstrates the framework's effectiveness. We performed WCET estimations and runtime measurements for both serial and parallel versions, confirming the framework's practicality and the significant parallelism achieved.

In the future, we plan to extend the framework's modeling and analysis capabilities for shared resources. Modern processors usually include e.g., shared L2 caches [8], [21], shared buses [22], etc., to further improve the performance, which may lead to overestimation of the analysis results if such sharing factors are not considered.

The final stage of WCET analysis combines control flow analysis and microprocessor modeling to compute the final WCET estimation. The most commonly used technique in this field is implicit path enumeration. The basic idea of this technique is to transform the WCET problem into one that determines the number of times each instruction is executed. This problem is then modeled as an integer linear programming problem, which can be solved efficiently.

note.p: 1) Control Flow Analysis: This process starts with the program's source code or object code, analyzing the program's logical structure, syntax, and semantics to identify all possible execution paths and extract the program's CFG. Control flow analysis focuses on extracting control flow information from the program and determining loop bounds. 2) Microprocessor Modeling: This involves considering the impact of low-level microprocessor features, such as pipeline and caching, on the program's execution time. The goal of microprocessor modeling is to estimate an upper bound on the WCET for each instruction in the CFG, given the specific characteristics of the processor. 3) WCET Computation:
